identity.title: ABCA1 deficiency exacerbates diet-induced atherosclerosis and hepatic xanthomatosis in knockout hamsters.

content.abstract: ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) is a critical transmembrane protein that mediates the cellular efflux of cholesterol and phospholipids to extracellular acceptors. Lipid metabolism dysfunctions caused by ABCA1 deficiency in humans have been closely linked to atherosclerotic disease. However, ABCA1 deficient mouse models reported so far are inadequate for faithfully recapitulating the characteristics of dyslipidemia and atherosclerotic pathology seen in ABCA1 deficient patients. To overcome this problem, we attempted to use a golden Syrian hamster model because of its lipid metabolism similarities to humans, and generated ABCA1 knockout (KO) hamsters using the CRISPR/Cas9 technique and examined the pathophysiological consequences of ABCA1 deficiency. On a normal chow diet, ABCA1 KO hamsters exhibited significantly lower levels of plasma total cholesterol (TC) but higher levels of plasma triglycerides (TG) compared with the wild-type (WT) controls. Nevertheless, plasma HDLs were nearly undetectable in KO hamsters. On a high-cholesterol high-fat diet, male KO hamsters displayed more pronounced hyperlipidemia with increased levels of plasma TC and TG compared with those in WT controls, a change attributable to a remarkable increase in TC contents in VLDLs and in TG contents in all apoB-containing lipoproteins, whereas cholesterol in IDLs and large LDLs was reduced. Female KO hamsters, in contrast, showed consistently lower plasma TC levels than WT controls. Pathological analysis showed that ABCA1 deficiency not only promoted aortic atherosclerosis but also caused massive hepatic xanthomatosis in KO hamsters. These results indicate that ABCA1 KO hamsters may become a useful model for the study of human dyslipidemia and atherosclerosis.
